issues.item: Triggers: Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'people who look similar to the victims' is clinically incoherent because the patient is the victim; a plausible trigger would be people resembling the perpetrator(s) or contextual robbery cues. As written, this item conflicts with the trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: Feeling dirty/contaminated is not impossible after robbery, but in this profile it is hard to reconcile with the rest of the selected items, which otherwise center on danger, self-blame, and moral injury rather than sexual violation or disgust-based trauma themes. This makes the appraisal set clinically inconsistent with the trauma context.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, 'Being naked' as a primary trigger is hard to reconcile unless there was a stripping/sexual humiliation element, which is not suggested elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items point to perpetrator proximity and assault cues, making this vulnerability trigger clinically incongruent with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' implies morally troubling behaviour during the event, but the rest of the profile reflects victim-focused danger, self-blame, and mistrust rather than any specific morally injurious action. In a mugging/robbery context this item is difficult to justify without corroborating memory/appraisal content about the patient's own behaviour.

vignette:
# Anahera's Story

Anahera was thirty-two when the mugging happened, a Tuesday evening in late September as she walked from the parking garage toward her apartment building in a neighborhood she had lived in for five years. She had been thinking about the quarterly reports due the next morning—her mind was at the office, not on the street—when she heard footsteps accelerating behind her. Before she could turn, a hand gripped her shoulder with such force that she felt her body wrench sideways. A man's voice, low and urgent, demanded her bag. She remembered the smell of stale cigarettes and sweat, the metallic taste of blood from where her teeth cut the inside of her cheek when he shoved her against the concrete wall. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. He took her purse and ran. A neighbor found her sitting on the curb ten minutes later, shaking but unharmed.

In the weeks that followed, Anahera returned to work, answered emails, paid bills. She told herself it was over. But by November, three months in, the world had fundamentally changed shape. Footsteps anywhere—in the office hallway, in the grocery store, behind her on the street—sent her into a state of hyperalert panic. The sound itself was enough to trigger a cascade of threat responses: her heart would race, her breathing would shallow, and she would find herself unable to believe that she was actually safe, even when her husband Marcus assured her that they were home with the doors locked. What made this worse was the way her mind had begun to reframe the attack itself. She had come to believe that the mugging happened because of who she was—careless, inattentive, the kind of person who walked alone lost in thought and invited predation. This conviction about her own culpability meant that every unexpected sound carried a deeper message: the world was dangerous, yes, but more importantly, she was vulnerable in a way that was her own fault. That belief about herself fed back into her threat perception, making it impossible to dismiss even routine noises as innocent. When the mailman knocked on the door, her pulse spiked. When Marcus came up behind her in the kitchen to embrace her, she would flinch violently, her body convinced it was happening again.

By early spring, Anahera had developed a set of strategies that seemed, in her mind, to offer some protection. She would deliberately dissociate when she felt unsafe—consciously trying to leave her body, to blank out the sensations that felt unbearable. She spent hours ruminating about how she could have prevented the attack: she should have taken a different route, should have been more aware, should have walked faster, should have screamed louder. These cycles of self-blame rumination would stretch across entire evenings, each iteration reinforcing her sense that the event was somehow her doing, which in turn deepened her conviction that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that she could not trust even Marcus's reassurances of safety. The rumination itself became a way of managing the unbearable feeling of powerlessness—if she could find the flaw in her own behavior, perhaps she could prevent it from happening again. But the rumination also kept her trapped in a loop where her negative beliefs about herself and the world grew more entrenched. When she tried to relax on a Saturday afternoon, she found it impossible; her body remained tensed, waiting for the next threat, certain that danger was imminent.

The memories themselves had taken on a surreal, almost hallucinatory quality. When they surfaced—often triggered by the sound of footsteps or an unexpected touch—she would find herself tasting blood again, feeling her body contort into the same twisted position against the wall. The vividness was so extreme that it seemed impossible this had actually happened to her; it felt like something from a film, too vivid and too terrible to be real. Yet that very unreality made the memories more frightening, not less. If her own mind could conjure something so intense, how could she trust her perception of safety at any moment? The memories would pull her back into that state of threat, her body rigid, her breathing shallow, and she would find herself dissociating again, trying to escape the sensations by blanking out, which only left her more disconnected from the present and more vulnerable to the next trigger.

At work, the impact had become undeniable. Anahera manages a team of four junior accountants, and by April she had begun avoiding the open office space. She would arrive early or stay late to work alone, unable to tolerate the unpredictability of colleagues approaching her desk or the sound of footsteps in the corridor. When a client meeting ran longer than scheduled, she found herself catastrophizing—assuming that the delay meant something had gone wrong, that she had made an error, that something bad was about to happen. Her supervisor had noticed the withdrawal. Her team had noticed it too. Marcus noticed it most of all: his wife, who used to laugh easily and reach for him without hesitation, now flinched at his touch and spent evenings staring at nothing, caught in loops of self-recrimination that he could not interrupt.

It was Marcus who finally insisted she see someone. "You're not living," he said quietly one evening in May. "You're just trying not to die." Anahera knew he was right. She sat in the intake appointment, describing the footsteps, the taste of blood, the absolute impossibility of believing she was safe, the certainty that she had brought this on herself through her own carelessness. What she wanted most was to stop being afraid. What she feared most was that she was fundamentally broken—that the person she had been before that September evening was someone the attack had revealed to be fragile and flawed, and that no amount of therapy could change that essential truth about who she was.
